There is also no speech and no banker search, and Dan co-owns a room whose exit lands at the guild house.

Out is the door's "Exit to House Steward", a teleport to the landing at (4134, 1429). That teleport starts the 60 s lockout and the Stationary Penalty, and both are walked off before the first chop. From there the runner recalls "as close to the lumbering spot as we can via rune tomes in the rune library or our own rune tomes/books" (the owner's rule; the landing choice is in §7). Home is always the default rune of Dan's own runebook, "DTF Loot Chest". Power words to arrival took 1.95–2.09 s over 34 live recalls harness/escape.py. At home the runner finds the house steward and walks its menu, "Room" → "Visit Other Rooms" → the owner's row. room.py never presses End Rental Contract.

In the room the logs come out of the hue-38 trapped pouch of the thief guard (§8). Dan sets it off himself, takes one hit, and converts each stack (one try per stack plus 3 retries). Since 2026-10-05 the boards go into the Resource Stockpile ("It is where we will now drop off all our boards", the owner), one target per stack, never ourselves, which "would add every valid item in the pack". After the chest's boards moved in, it read 8,693. Restock and Resupply at the room shelf then return the spent pouch, and "Dan keeps exactly the loadout". The first live trip of this design (10-04, 22:06–22:17, Horseshoe Bay) chopped 209 logs at 11 stands in 527 s and stored 240 boards (with 11 logs from the aborted first attempt and Harvest Aspect doubles). It then took 9.5 s to enter the room, 14.7 s to convert and 4.1 s to store.

6.8Testing from captures

test_loop_lumber.py (3,109 lines) puts the real proxy in front of a simulated server. The simulator speaks the demo's packet shapes and the room's captured menus, and a scripted "human" answers CAPTCHAs. It serves decoys on every attempt, one solver-readable and one unreadable real CAPTCHA, a door that swings shut and moongates whose renounce prompt must be closed. The main run's two trips assert the invariants. The agent goes out by the door and in by the steward. It replies only to the CAPTCHA, gate prompts, runebook and room menus. It sends no speech at all, and every log not stolen ends up stored.

The working rule was that every live incident becomes a scenario that fails against the old code. The suite now holds 22 end-to-end scenarios, each in its own process with private ports, up to 8 in parallel (about 2 min critical path, 10 min serial). It also holds 12 unit checks, some of which replay live captures through the world model with no simulator (Table 12).

6.9Failures and pivots

The first evening alone brought four live attempts and four fixes. The overworld deaths behind later entries are in §8.

  1. 2026-09-29 21:23Lost upstairs. The room exit dropped TestWorth on an inn's upper floor, where 2-D walk memory failed after 21 blocked moves. The owner's directive, "the full x/y/z Outlands map", produced the map decode and pathfinder within the hour.
  2. 2026-09-29 22:10NPCs as walls. Two NPCs in a hallway made all 8 trees "unreachable". The owner noted that "in UOO you shove through mobiles", so mobiles became a cost rather than a wall.
  3. 2026-09-29 22:27First full trip: 46 boards stored, after fixing vendor range and a random CAPTCHA button id. Run 3 stored 50 boards in 8 min 25 s, about 355 logs per trip-hour.
  4. 2026-09-29 23:04Chopping from a cave. The agent stood at z −20 under trees at z 5. The server allowed it, but "a player in that cave can't see or click a tree on the surface". Goals became height-aware.
  5. 2026-10-02Survivorship bias. Only trips that reached the bank had been recorded, which "flattered exactly the spots where trips get cut short". The episode row moved into finally.
  6. 2026-10-04Smart Harvest, the room again, script pace. Two false alarms followed. The Harvest Aspect's proc effect was read as a spell on us, and a new run saw the previous run's own pouch pop as a theft.
  7. 2026-10-05A day of fixes. The Wintertop death, a stuck conversion, bad landings, aggro zones, the stockpile and Restock. Each fix came with a scenario.

Lesson

The demonstration bought exact ids; it could not show other floors, crowded hallways, caves under trees, monsters or thieves. Each of those gaps surfaced live, got fixed once and was pinned by a test.

7Self-optimization: where to chop and how much to carry

The runner works one spot; a pure-function planner decides which spot, how many logs per trip and which hatchet, using a small Bayesian model of place, character and danger, a renewal-reward trip size and Thompson sampling. In its latest snapshot it is deliberately exploring: no spot has more than a 2.4% chance of being the best, and nearly every trip is sized by the grove, not by the hazards.

7.1Objective and architecture

The objective: boards stored at home per agent-active hour, net of expected losses docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md:177. One log makes one board. Pacing is a floor, not a knob: the optimizer picks places and trip sizes but never tightens the delays, breaks or daily cap that the runners' pacing rules fix.

harness/lumber_opt.py (1,602 lines; first commit 5a33805, 2026-10-02 23:26) is a pure function plan(...) over plain lists, fed by plan_from_store. It returns one runner command, e.g. ctl run lumber --spot witcher_219 --trips 1 --logs-per-trip 2360 --regrow-min 65 --timeout 8270, so "the overseer, a future daemon or a human run the same decision" docs/PLAN.md:488-489. The Seer (§9) asks ctl lumber plan before each run.

7.2Spots, recency and the character

A spot is only a place: an area, its trees, a PvP flag and a hazard_prior. Since 2026-10-04 every trip starts and ends at home, so getting there is not part of it. Evidence is weighted by recency, so shifts in competition, killers or patches show up within weeks:

wi=0.5agei/14 days
(5)

Place and character are modelled separately. Outland Dan's Lumberjacking rose from 50.1 to 81.2 in about a day (§10), so a plain per-spot average would favour whichever spots were visited last. The success chance per attempt follows the wiki, summed over the ten wood colours a tree can be:

A hatchet's material and quality add a tool bonus that multiplies the chance: Exceptional +0.04, Bronze +0.08, Avarite +0.18 docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md:81-82.
p(S,b)=min⁡(1, ∑jbasej100clip[0,1]⁡(S−offj′divj′(1+b))),j′=j if S≥minj, else ordinary
(6)

S is skill, b the tool bonus, basej the chance a tree is wood j (81.75% ordinary to 0.25% avarwood); a colour above our skill counts as ordinary, an inference the code flags harness/lumber_opt.py:337-356. It checks out: Hackworth at 69.1 hit 44/63 at Terran (0.70) against 0.69 predicted docs/NOTES.md:362-364. Each trip's chopping time tc is rescaled to today's chance; walking is not:

Hadj=max⁡(F−tc+tcpthen/pnow, 0.1F),Hadj≥0.25 h for a place failure
(7)

with F the field time. The floor makes a trip the place spoiled (no reachable tree, a town region) cost a quarter hour at zero logs, so a dud spot loses its optimistic prior harness/lumber_opt.py:499-510. The Harvest Aspect (armour that sometimes doubles a yield) is left to recency weighting.

7.3Field rate and overhead

The field rate λs is logs per field hour, walking between trees included. Logs come in lumps (7.82 per success over 2,400 successes), so trips scatter far beyond Poisson; a quasi-Poisson dispersion ϕ (Pearson χ2/dof over trips of 3+ minutes, floor 8) was 14 on 2026-10-02 and 26.8 at the snapshot harness/lumber_opt.py:725-742. Discounting the evidence by ϕ:

λs∼Gamma(α0+1ϕ∑iwiLi,  β0+1ϕ∑iwiHadj,i),α0=μ2/s02,  β0=μ/s02
(8)

The prior is empirical Bayes: μ is the mean rate of spots with half a weighted field hour, s02=max⁡(Var⁡ˆ,(0.35μ)2), and 1,200 logs per field hour before any data harness/lumber_opt.py:825-838. An unvisited spot is "a spot like the others", explored but not trusted. Tree density was rejected as a prior term ("it didn't predict logs per field hour across the 7 spots with trips"); it returns as capacity.

Overhead T is everything but chopping. Its prior, in seconds:

T0=10⏟room exit+0.45(library walk+walk in)+2⋅4⏟recalls+60⏟lockout+15⏟into room+40⏟convert, store
(9)

The posterior is a weighted Normal counting the prior as one observation; the per-trip spread is floored at 30 s and the posterior sd is that spread over n, so it can fall below 30 s harness/lumber_opt.py:704-722, 857-862. Overheads are short: 102 s at Horseshoe Bay, 135 s at witcher_23.

7.4Three ways a trip ends early

The rewrite of 2026-10-03 (86075f3) split danger into three competing hazards per field hour, each a per-spot Gamma posterior over weighted exposure, shrunk to a pooled rate:

  • Death hD: nothing stored, every unblessed item lost, plus an inferred R=20 minutes of recovery.
  • Sent home hS: a recall escape, guard flight or creature stop (§8); the load comes home.
  • Theft hT: a thief takes a share f∼Beta(1,1) of the load and the trip goes on.

Deaths are rare, so their prior is built from commoner events: hostile sightings per field hour σs, times a pooled π=P(death|sighting), plus a pooled creature-death rate hC:

hD∼Gamma(10m0+∑w⋅died, 10+Es),m0=σsπ[pvp]+hC,π∼Beta(1+pkw, 3+seenw−pkw)
(10)

Es is weighted field hours. A death counts against a spot if it falls in a trip there or within 30 minutes after ("the Terran PK killed us 11 s after the runner stopped") harness/lumber_opt.py:517-551, 892-915, 1119-1126. Prior strengths are in Table 13. The same PK deaths count twice: in the pooled π prior and in the spot's own death count harness/lumber_opt.py:869, 894-895, 1119. That empirical-Bayes double use makes hD at the death spots (Terran, witcher_23, witcher_282) somewhat overconfident while deaths are this few.

7.5How much to carry: from a square root to renewal-reward

On 2026-09-29, before the first live trip, we set the return trigger with a textbook inventory argument: at r logs per minute, overhead T and death hazard hD, the cost per stored log is

cost(Q)=rTQ+hDQ2r+hDTback⇒Q∗=r2T/hD
(11)

The rule's hazard is death only, "PK encounters × P(death)" docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md:190: being sent home loses nothing, so it has no place in a cost per stored log, and with hD+hS the rule would give sizes of 252–590. Its flaws, named at the rewrite: it credited a dying trip with Q/2 banked, its expected deaths hDQ/λ exceed 1 on long trips, and Q sat on a 60-minute stint cap docs/PLAN.md:501-504. The replacement treats a trip as one renewal-reward cycle (Figure 22). Chopping Q logs takes tf=Q/λ; with h=hD+hS and theft thinning the load at k=hTf:

C(t)=λ(1−e−kt)k,B(Q)=e−htfC(tf)+hS∫0tfe−htC(t)dt,PD=hD∫0tfe−htdt,𝔼[time]=T+∫0tfe−htdt+RPD,Rate(Q)=B(Q)−supplies−GPD𝔼[time]
(12)

G is the gear at risk (unblessed items at replacement price); it and the supplies are priced in logs at the board price. Every integral has a closed form, so PD≤1 for any Q; that is why "a clamp on deaths" and Monte Carlo per Q were both rejected docs/PLAN.md:509-510. best_q scans 41 log-spaced sizes from 200 to 10,000 logs plus the weight cap, then refines by golden section to 10 logs harness/lumber_opt.py:797-822.

Finding

The square-root rule was not far off. At the snapshot's means its Q is 2–16% below the renewal-reward optimum (Horseshoe Bay 1,810 vs 2,160; witcher_23 2,077 vs 2,350; Terran 1,020 vs 1,040; witcher_291 870 vs 1,010), which costs under 0.1% of the rate in our recomputation. The rewrite fixed the accounting, not the size: at Q∗, P(death) per trip is 3–10% but P(sent home) is 58–83%. Threats, not deaths, end most long trips.

That shapes the curves: being sent home costs only the next trip's overhead, so "being sent home alone never shrinks Q (nothing is lost); deaths, thefts and the gear at risk do" docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md:336-337. On the 2026-10-03 store the rewrite changed sizes by up to ×1.6 on eligible spots (×2.2 on the Young-only Shelter spot), mostly by lifting them off the stint cap, and net rates fell as sent-home stops were charged honestly docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md:395-407.

7.6Grove capacity and regrowth

The owner's point on 2026-10-03: a sparse grove dries up sooner, so its trip pays full overhead for fewer logs. The runner ends a trip dry once its listed trees are chopped, so a trip holds at most

grove_logs=avail×ψ×Ltree,ψ∼Beta(10ψ0+y, 10(1−ψ0)+n−y),ψ0=∑y+1∑n+2
(13)

avail counts tree tiles not depleted, unreachable or marked out of wood within the regrowth window, y of n tried tiles ever yielded, and Ltree is 19.3 logs per tree cycle, pooled over 471 cycles (17.7–20.2 per spot) harness/lumber_opt.py:622-689. The yielding share ψ varies, 0.47 at witcher_282 to 0.86 at corpse_creek at the snapshot (0.46 to 0.85 on 2026-10-03), and the model matched dry trips (Horseshoe Bay ~677 predicted, dry at 605 and 613). When the cap binds, the run is one trip, and the runner gets the uncapped Q∗ "so it chops until the trees really run out instead of stopping at the estimate" (aa1de12).

Regrowth comes from pairs of a depleted answer followed by a later try on the same tree. A pool-adjacent-violators isotonic fit gives P(regrown|gap); the window is the first block reaching 0.6, rounded up to 5 minutes harness/lumber_opt.py:578-619. It replaced a 20-minute guess that "sent the runner to depleted trees".

Since Smart Harvest (2026-10-04) the server picks the tree, so new data adds no regrowth pairs or tried tiles harness/lumber_opt.py:585-587, 631-634.

The estimate is biased upward by design: "Retry gaps shorter than the window in use are no longer observed, so the estimate can only move up from here unless the window is shortened on purpose" docs/NOTES.md:359-361.

7.7Choosing a spot: Thompson sampling

For each eligible spot the planner draws (λ,T,σs,π,hD,hS,hT,ψ) once, takes maxQ⁡Rate over every other grid point, and the best draw wins. Repeating this 2,000 times gives each spot's P(best); the pick is labelled explore when it is not the best by posterior mean harness/lumber_opt.py:1213-1226. The theft share f and the creature rate hC are not drawn: both enter the mean plan and every draw as pooled posterior means harness/lumber_opt.py:908-915. Spots are ineligible for 30 minutes after a death or player threat, 20 after a thief, until regrowth after a dry trip, and 7 days after two place failures in a row.

Decision

Thompson sampling "explores in proportion to how likely a spot is to be the best, needs no tuning constant, and varies the routine". Rejected: ε-greedy ("explores bad spots as often as promising ones, needs an ε schedule"), UCB ("deterministic, so the same spot order every day; a fixed pattern is a bot signature") and an LLM reading the stats ("not reproducible, no uncertainty accounting") docs/PLAN.md:482-489.

Variation is required, not an inefficiency to remove.

— docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md §6, "Anti-pattern guard"

Discovery. ctl lumber discover turned three seed spots into 132. It counts trees in 29×29-tile windows on a global 7-tile lattice within 200 tiles of each Witcher rune (a public library of 360 wilderness runes, 359 table ids plus a duplicate 83; §4) with a summed-area table, ranks windows across runes, and keeps those with 25+ trees, a walk of at most 300 tiles and distance from towns and guard points harness/lumber_opt.py:1456-1585. The first search looked 21 tiles out, and "212 of 360 runes had too few trees". On 2026-10-03 the owner approved all 125 candidates not named after monsters at once: "heavy exploration is the point of the Thompson sampler" docs/PLAN.md:520-537.

Landing. A trip recalls to the rune nearest the grove that has a walking route in, from the home library or our own books, skipping monster-named runes, the "Bad Places" tome and remembered bad landings harness/lumber_opt.py:194-211. The owner's rule: "always recall as close to the lumbering spot as we can … never public moongates or starting at banks and walking".

7.8Hatchets, wear and the price of a board

Each hatchet we own or could buy at a known price rescales the rate through the chopping share ρ of field time, minus wear at one use per success:

λ′=(ρλpnowp(b)+1−ρλ)−1,value=v−vlogs/success⋅priceuses⋅1gp/log
(14)

where v=maxQ⁡Rate(λ′), with a bought hatchet's price added to G harness/lumber_opt.py:1023-1039. One use per success was measured twice (a hatchet went 500 → 163 over 337 chops on 2026-10-05). Wear is small: an iron hatchet (25 gp, 500 uses) at 1,700 net logs per trip-hour costs about 11 gp, 0.4 logs, per hour. The bonus is not: the exceptional, mastercrafted bronze hatchet Dan was handed on 2026-10-05 (+0.16; docs/NOTES.md:578-584) lifts p at 80.1 skill from 0.776 to 0.900, about 11% more logs per field hour at a 0.7 chop share. Every carried hatchet is lost on death, so a bought one is "worth it where nobody can kill us, not where they can". Unpriced hatchets get a break-even price instead.

Gold becomes logs at board:ordinary: the wiki's 9.5 gp until 2026-10-05, when the lowest commodity ask put it at 26.8 gp (134,000 gp per 5,000-board deed), and coloured woods were mostly no dearer (dullwood 22, copperwood 20, bronzewood 19; only shadowwood, at 30 gp, beat ordinary). Valued at the 2026-10-05 asks instead of the wiki's 9.5 gp, the 63 trip rows' 16,036 logs went from 147,773 to 428,442 gp (ba7ade5, b2238c7); that basis prices the 3,252 logs without a wood breakdown as ordinary, while §10 values only the 12,784 logs with one, about 341k gp. For the planner, gear and supplies got cheaper in logs: a 200 gp recall charge is 7.5 logs, not 21.

7.9A snapshot of the planner

We ran plan_from_store read-only at 2026-10-05 20:26 (no live character, cached routes, seed 1). Skill from the last trip row was 80.1 (p=0.776); pooled π=0.193, creature deaths hC 0.046 and sent home 2.54 per field hour, thefts 0.015 (prior only), regrowth 65 minutes, rate prior 2,316 logs per field hour (CV 0.40). The creature rate is a posterior (prior 0.01/h over 20 pseudo-hours) that counts only D11 of Dan's three 10-05 deaths: D9 was read as a PK, D10 fell outside its spot; raw, that is 1 attributed creature death in 7.2 field hours.

132spots (128 eligible, 26 with a trip)
0.024highest P(best), an unvisited spot
119 / 128eligible spots grove-bound
≈88%of P(best) held by never-visited spots

The pick was witcher_219, explore, P(best) 0.006: its grove holds an estimated 470 logs, so one trip with an uncapped quota of 2,360, about 15 minutes, 357 boards expected, P(death)=0.022, P(sent home)=0.40. The greedy best, witcher_23 (net 2,596 logs/trip-h at its grove-capped Q; field rate 3,483 logs per field hour over 3 trips), has P(best) 0.007. With 105 eligible never-visited spots sharing a prior wide enough to reach the best measured rates, the sampler spreads its bets thin; on 2026-10-05 Dan went to a new spot on 20 of 27 trips (§10). Visits measured less than they suggest: 26 of the 132 spots had a trip (27 with Shelter Island, no longer a spot), but only 14 of the 26 have any field time. The other 12 had only trips that ended before chopping, keep the prior 2,316 [1,246–3,540] and hold P(best) like unvisited spots, while the six well-measured spots (Horseshoe Bay, Terran, witcher_282, corpse_creek, witcher_291, witcher_280) all have P(best) = 0. And trip size is now set by the groves, which are smaller than Q∗, not by the hazards.

Caveat

Much of the danger model is still prior: the one observed theft (10-03, Caputo Wood) was never booked as a theft event, so hT and f are pure prior, and R and the room terms of T0 are guesses. One aborted trip is a false hazard sample, a Harvest-Aspect sparkle read as a spell docs/NOTES.md:602-607. The snapshot is not a live plan either: without a proxy the gear at risk is the last row's iron hatchet, and only cached landing routes count.

8Staying alive

The harness never fights a player, so survival is a matter of noticing early and leaving fast. This chapter shows how it tells a player killer from a goat, how the escape grew from “stop” to a recall that recasts until it lands, and how each of eleven deaths became a rule within hours. It also covers the thief guard, the staff alarm, the CAPTCHA solver and the one runner that is allowed to fight.

11character deaths, 09-30 → 10-05 (3 to one player killer)
8 / 10player-triggered escape recalls landed (both failures Bastet, old 3-try code)
53 / 53CAPTCHAs accepted, 0 strikes
0deaths in 36 hunt-runner visits (173 kills)

8.1The stance: never fight back

Notoriety is the colour of a name: blue innocent, grey attackable or criminal, orange enemy, red murderer, yellow invulnerable (code 7). A PK (player killer) is a red who kills other players for their loot. See §2.

The threat research of 2026-09-29 opens with one rule: “The harness never attacks a player.” Hitting a player brings Heat of Battle, which blocks recall (the one fast way out), makes you criminal and draws staff attention docs/research/THREATS.md §0. Everything below is detection and evasion, never retaliation.

The data for that evasion came partly from accidents and partly on purpose:

Let's bank what we've got and go somewhere potentially more dangerous and see if we can get PK'd or killed by mobs for science (data to improve our agent harness)

— the owner, viz chat to the overseer, 2026-10-02 17:27

Two hours later a red named Bastet killed Hackworth in the Terran wilds, and the owner replied by phone: “that's exactly the data we were hoping for”.

8.2Reading a mobile: the threat classifier

Outlands gives no clean “this is a PK” signal. Monsters show grey, mongbats turn criminal, human-bodied NPCs exist, and a pickpocket is blue until he steals. threats.assess() is a pure function of one state snapshot, so it can be unit-tested and replayed over captures harness/threats.py.

identify() decides what a mobile is, in order: a ghost is ignored; notoriety 7 is an NPC; mobile flag 0x20 or a “(Young)” label makes a player; a non-human body named “a/an …” is a monster; a “Name the title” label is an NPC; a human body with a creature name and no flag is a monster at notoriety 3 (the orc-hunter fix, 0add311). Any other human body counts as a player. The 0x20 flag is an empirical find: by 10-04 it was on 1,474 human mobiles at notoriety 1/3/4/6 and never on 2,607 notoriety-7 sightings or about 2,400 non-humans docs/PLAN.md "Staff alarm".

Movement turns Chebyshev distance into an arrival estimate, ETA=max⁡(0,d−rs)⋅s, with s = 0.2 s/tile for a player running, 0.1 mounted and 0.4 for a monster, and strike range rs = 12 tiles for a player (an assumption: RunUO's spell range; the Outlands value is unsourced), 1 for a monster. The flee radius is the distance at which a recall still lands first:

Rflee=rs+⌊trecall+tmargins⌋
(15)

The design example, a 4 s recall and 1 s margin against a red on foot, gives 12 + 25 = 37 tiles, past the 18-tile view, “so any visible red means flee”. The deployed runner uses a 2 s recall and 1 s margin: 27 tiles against a red on foot, 42 against a mounted one.

Creatures are judged by aggression: swinging or casting at us, war-mode flag 0x40 unless the body or name is on a passive list, known aggressive bodies, else not aggressive. That default changed on 09-30 after lumber trips stopped for a walrus and a goat c7dc39c.

Damage was harder than it sounds. “Outlands has never sent one with us as the defender”: all 3,638 swing packets (0x2F) in the store at the snapshot (2,172 when this was found on 10-03) are our own, so the live damage signal is the hits trend. Spells are caught by their visual effects on us or by lines such as “Magic reflect removed.”; all 93 such signals in the captures came with an attack. Since the server never names an attacker, hit_attackers blames adjacent creatures first, then ranged ones in reach, then anything within 12 tiles.

8.3Bastet, three times

The same red killed Hackworth three times in 24 hours, and each encounter broke a different assumption (Figure 27).

Terran wilds, 10-02 19:43. Bastet rode into view at 18 tiles. The runner aborted at 0.29 s and then stood still: its only response to danger was an Unsafe stop. “Bastet is attacking you!” came at 2.80 s; the first hit at 4.58 s carried a hamstring (no running for about 3 s); five hits and 102 damage later Hackworth was dead at 10.96 s. The “5…1” countdown over Bastet's head was most likely an explosion-potion fuse inferred: a blast followed 1.2 s after “1”, after the death: “Weapon, not explosion.” Tracking never fired, and the runner's ETA guess of 0.6 s was eight times too pessimistic docs/NOTES.md "Bastet".

That last number flipped the design. The one live runebook recall on record took 2.09 s from button to arrival, and Bastet needed 4.58 s from sight to first hit. “So a recall started within ~2.4 s of sight lands before the first hit. … A recall is the only action with a chance, so it wins.” Recall-on-sight shipped at 22:16 that night f7aab09.

Nusero, 10-03 18:04. Bastet appeared at 11 tiles carrying the Stationary Penalty, which suggests he had just recalled in or had stood hidden inferred. The new escape reacted fast, starting a recall at 1.05 s, but his Weaken landed at 1.88 s and broke it. The instant retry was refused as “not recovered”, his Harm broke the third try, and the three-try escape gave up at 3.64 s. Then nothing hit Hackworth for 4.5 s (Bastet's potion blew on his own tile, two swings missed), and no escape was running to use it. The verdict: “A mage PK who recalls onto us beats a 2 s recall escape”.

The commit and NOTES say Bastet “struck 5.5 s later” after the tracking hit. The DB event clock gives 6.51 s to “attacking you” and 7.59 s to the first hit. We suspect the note was rounded from a different anchor.

Terran wilds again, 10-03 19:08. This time Tracking reported “Bastet (55 spaces to target)”, but the react range was 40 tiles, so it was only logged. He came into view 4.57 s later, during the chop's 2.1 s aim pause. The runner answered the chop cursor first and opened the tome 2.5 s after sight; the first hit at 3.02 s broke the cast, and Hackworth died at 8.39 s. The real bug: “The runner was blind inside every pause and result wait”, because Human.wait was a plain sleep c4db365. The owner first asked by phone for a 60-tile react range; offered 40, 80 or any by the agent, he chose 80 4017175.

8.4The escape, v1 to v3

The escape (harness/escape.py) presses the default rune's charge in the runebook or rune tome and falls back to casting Recall. It was rebuilt twice, each time from measurements.

v2 (10-03 18:27) came from a study of the casts in the store docs/research/SPELL_INTERRUPTS.md. Recall takes a median 2.03 s from power words to arrival (1.95–2.09 s, 27 casts). Creature melee breaks a cast 44% of the time (26/59), damage-over-time ticks never (0/13), Bastet 3/3. After a disturbed cast, all 30 live retries fit RunUO's pre-AOS recovery rule, where e is how far into the cast it broke and T the cast time:

trec=max⁡(0.2,1−e/T) s
(16)

So v2 has no try limit, only a 20 s budget, and presses each retry the moment recovery ends. Replayed on Nusero, the old code gives up 2.73 s after the double-click (live: 2.72 s); the new one lands at 5.0 s d6e6c63. “A PK has to land a fresh interrupt within every 2 s cast, and giving up hands him the time.”

v3 (10-05) learned the failure that killed Outland Dan at Wintertop, “This book needs time to recharge.”: a recharging book is now answered by casting Recall on the book itself, which worked live at 10:59 87b53fe.

In the store, 18 of 20 logged lumber escape recalls landed (17 of them 2.09–2.16 s from press to arrival); both logged failures were Bastet, under the old three-try code. D9's escape failed before a cast (a recharging book) and is not in that count. Of the 10 player-triggered escape recalls, 8 landed; a pk_escape juncture is written only after a successful escape, so the eight such junctures (the last four on 10-05, when Tracking finally reported reds at 35–64 tiles) are clean by construction. If a recall fails off guarded ground, a guard flight runs A* to guard points learned from “now protected” notices at the tile where they appeared 4cb8b9c.

8.5Eleven deaths and what each one bought

Figure 28 and Table 14 list every death, near-death, theft and costly false alarm. The memory store holds 10 death events; the eleventh, TestWorth's planned demo (09-30 10:18), is in a stored session but predates the death event. Three were Bastet, three the overseer acting by hand, three monsters on runner trips, one a blind long walk, one the demo. 10-03 alone had five.

The overseer deaths taught the bluntest lesson. At Urukton Bluffs the recall-in had knocked Shackleworth's arcane staff into his pack; the overseer walked about 85 steps into an orc room and fought bare-fisted for 2 damage a blow while losing about 6 hit points a second.

Yeah no manual fights in dungeons is a good rule. An LLM is way too slow to react for combat.

— the owner, omp session, 2026-10-03 20:31

Lesson

Early on, false positives cost trips: a walrus, a goat, a battle trainer. By 10-05, false negatives were killing Dan: an unknown failure message, a house door in an escape route, an 8.93 s humanizing pause. Each fix made the runner more cautious; lumber flee events rose from 2–13 a day (09-30 → 10-04) to 31 on 10-05, the price of the owner's final policy: “run and recall until home, never stopping in the field”.

8.6Thieves: step away, and a trapped pouch

At 100 Stealing a thief takes about 200 logs per grab, once every 5 s, from 1 tile away. The one we met, Caputo Wood, was blue until the instant the reagents left the pack (T1). The owner's summary, “thieves look friendly to us until they steal, and so a friendly player being within 2 tiles of us AT ALL while we're lumbering is almost certainly a thief”, became the 2-tile rule 2516411. Attacking him is out, so the guard has three layers ad5a6c0:

  1. Keep-away. The runner pauses as if reading, then walks to ≥ 4 tiles: “One step beats the 5 s steal cooldown, where a 2 s recall would still leave them in reach.” If he closes again: recall, and a 20-minute cooldown on that spot.
  2. Trapped pouch. Logs go into a trapped pouch after each chop. Its pop was decoded from our own set-off (hue 38 → 0, an explosion effect, a sound, −1 hit) a929050; a pop we did not cause is an alarm. “A pouch is a delay plus an alarm, not a lock.”
  3. Ledger. Losses become theft events that feed the optimizer's theft hazard (§7).

Live, keep-away fired twice on 10-05, both for mounted blues at 2 tiles. Neither came closer and nothing was stolen; we suspect passers-by. The only pouch alarm so far was F2, a false one.

8.7Staff: an alarm that has never rung for real

Staff are the one encounter the agent must not handle alone: “a player unresponsive to a GM for ~2 minutes while gathering is jailed, then banned on repeat.” Since 09-30 anyone speaking nearby holds a harvest job until a human or the overseer acks 38c427d, and staff hints in that speech raise gm_suspected with a repeating alarm 021bcec. On 10-04 the owner suggested a GM is probably an invulnerable player, so sight alone should alarm. Notoriety 7 alone would have fired in 12 of 13 lumber sessions, mostly on player vendors; notoriety 7 with flag 0x20 had never been seen (Table 15) 8e9cff7.

No staff_sighting exists in the store, and no staff alarm has fired since 10-02. A GM shown blue or grey, or hidden, would still get past the sight rule, so the speech hold remains the backstop.

8.8The CAPTCHA solver

Harvesting raises a CAPTCHA every 5–10 minutes, and three wrong answers mean a 6-hour harvest block, so a wrong answer is far more expensive than a slow one. The policy is that a human answers by default (the runner pauses and beeps) and the solver sits behind a toggle in the viz header. Here we cover the solver's design and its record. It needs no OCR: the digits arrive as dot glyphs placed in the gump layout, so the packet already carries the shapes, and the solver matches each one against a small reference font captured from earlier CAPTCHAs (Figure 29).

The confidence margin is the safety mechanism, and calibration showed its limit. With the only real 9 held out, the solver “confidently misreads 194 as 184”: “the margin gate guards ambiguity, not a digit shape the font has never seen”. A gate can refuse an ambiguous reading; it cannot know that a glyph is new. So the reference font kept growing, from 22 references (21 captured digits) at launch to 79 by the end of 10-03, when leave-one-session-out scoring was 26/26.

The outcome: 53 real CAPTCHAs, 53 answers, 53 “Captcha successful.”, 0 strikes. The solver answered 43 (median 13.25 s) and a human in the client answered 10 (median 10.21 s). We suspect the shard simply never uses 0, which would explain why we never captured a real one.

8.9The one runner that fights: hunt loop and crawl

After the overseer let Hackworth fall to 2/96, fighting moved into a deterministic runner, loop_hunt.py f5008fd. Each tick it takes the first of Leave → Speech hold → Heal → Stationary Penalty → Loot → Fight → Idle that applies. It leaves for a hostile player within 12 tiles, for two or more attackers below 80% hits, or below 60% plus a margin for the walk out, and heals with a potion when it can, else by spell.

The Stationary Penalty is an Outlands debuff: it appeared 301.0–314.8 s after the last step in all 40 measured cases, and 5 steps clear it.

One fight spot yields only 0.4–0.5 kills a minute and invites the Stationary Penalty, so the crawl patrols the New Player Dungeon instead ee62f02. Its floor graph has 10,829 tiles, up to 182 route steps deep, cut into five depth zones with 147 waypoints. Zone 1 starts at the store's measured 23.4 hits lost per minute; each deeper zone's prior is the one above times a depth risk of 1.5; and a zone opens only when its predicted damage is at most 30 hits/min. Since 23.4×1.5=35.1>30, zone 2 stays shut until zone 1 proves cheaper than about 20 hits/min.

Across 10-02 and 10-03 the hunt runner made 36 visits (265.7 minutes) for 173 kills and 2,785 gold. It left 32 times (18 for low hits, 9 for multiple attackers, 5 done) and died 0 times. The crawl has run live in zone 1 only.

8.10What still kills us

Nusero set the open problem: a stealthing mage who appears at 11 tiles and casts within 1.9 s beats a 2.03 s recall. docs/PLAN.md "PK survival" lists three answers. Detecting stealthers: Hackworth's Tracking sees hidden players only within about 8 tiles. Magic Reflection: at Nusero it would have bounced the Weaken, and recall 1 would have landed 0.49 s before his Harm; Hackworth lumbered with it up on the evening of 10-03, when it absorbed a gazer larva's spell (N3). Mounted flight with scripted healing helps only with a guard zone or line-of-sight break in reach. None has met a real PK yet. The system survives the threats it has met, and it learned each one by dying to it first.

9The Seer: an LLM on the outer loop

The language model never plays the game. It sits one loop out: it wakes on a database row, reads the situation through a JSON command-line tool, picks the next deterministic runner and handles the exceptions.

9.1From an API daemon to an agent that waits

At 17:08 on 2026-09-29 the owner chose a standalone Python loop on the Anthropic API for the agent runtime ("this is our own harness after all"), choosing skills and never raw packets session log 2026-09-29; docs/PLAN.md:59, committed 17:10. It lasted six hours. At 23:21 the owner sent a ten-point bedtime brief whose first point replaced it:

Tasks stay programmatic but an agent oversees them, and can get awoken at important junctures… we could keep using omp (Oh My Pi, this coding harness) and just make a CLI… not sure how we'd 'yield' back to the AI at important junctures in that case.

— the owner, 2026-09-29 23:21

The answer, committed at 23:47 49d433d: an omp session drives harness/ctl.py, the SQLite store is the bus, and the yield is ctl wait, a blocking call run as a background shell job. The daemon was "rejected for now" and could later replace omp on the same bus docs/PLAN.md:190-191.

The brief's first sentence stuck. Chopping, walking, fighting and storing are deterministic runners with their own guards, because "an LLM in the inner loop would be slow, costly and harder to keep stock-identical" docs/OVERSEER.md §1. The overseer reacts in a poll (~1 s) plus a model turn; anything that can't wait tens of seconds belongs to a runner. We learned it twice anyway. On 10-01 the overseer's improvised fight loop let Hackworth fall to 2 of 96 hit points among mongbats, and a programmatic hunt task replaced it that night f5008fd. On 10-03 a subagent fought by hand in Urukton Bluffs; the recall cast had knocked Shackleworth's staff out of his hands, and he died 15 s after one manual act attack, swinging his fists.

Decision

"Never fight by hand in a dungeon (user decision 2026-10-03): an LLM reacts far too slowly for combat … In dungeons only ctl run hunt fights; you scout, choose where it runs and watch." The same goes for lumbering: the Seer runs the planner's command verbatim, because "hand-picked arguments spoil the data" (§7).

Figure 31 shows the control plane.

9.2The juncture bus and ctl wait

The bus is three tables in harness.db. junctures(id, t, source, kind, severity, summary, data, acked_t) is what runners want the overseer to know; chat holds the conversation (kinds message, thought, action, memory); meta holds tasks, cursors and a heartbeat. There are no queues, only cursors, one set per consumer, so each is restart-safe alone.

Runners post threat, pk_escape, captcha, death, speech_nearby (the job holds until acked), gm_suspected (a staff alarm repeats until acked) and rarer kinds; the task wrapper posts task_done/task_failed. ctl wait polls once a second and returns on an open juncture above its cursor with severity ≥ attention, on any task end, on a new user chat row, or when its timeout runs out, at most 20 events per wake harness/ctl.py:107-109. The "any task end" clause was the first bug of live use: on 09-30 an info-level task_done didn't wake the overseer, which "sat idle after its trip" until a fix landed about four minutes after the task ended, two minutes after the owner noticed b264824. The coding agent told the stranded overseer through the bus itself, with an ad-hoc notice kind.

task_wrap.py removes a finished task from meta.tasks before posting its juncture, so a woken overseer can start the next run at once. While a run is on, the prompt has the Seer wake every ~150 s (ctl wait --timeout 150) to read the status and the task log docs/OVERSEER.md:496-497, since 7a48fd5; only an idle Seer makes no tool calls and spends no tokens between junctures, with the shell job finishing as the interrupt.

9.3ctl as the agent's API

Every overseer move is a ctl subcommand that prints one JSON object and exits 0 iff ok (Table 16). The guard rails live in the API, not the prompt: act accepts 29 whitelisted names and refuses raw packets, any act while a task runs, the captcha gump and button-less (honeypot-shaped) gumps. attack targets only hostile monsters, never below 30% hits; buy is capped at 50,000 gp a day. Free-text speech is allowed only during a speech_nearby hold, at most 120 characters, and must pass a regex that refuses words like bot, script, ai, proxy, claude or test harness/ctl.py:96-101. Every act mirrors a stock client gesture and is logged as a chat action.

Most of it grew on demand. The first live overseer, on 09-30, kept reporting "ctl has no …" and would not work around its rules: "I'm not allowed to edit the harness myself; I've asked the main agent to add an unequip/equip act to ctl. Holding still here until it lands." Each gap became a commit that day. Asked to farm gold by killing monsters, it declined under its no-attack rule; the owner overruled it within a minute, and the new policy was committed about five minutes later a0d78f7.

9.4The prompt and the persona

docs/OVERSEER.md §5 is the operating prompt, and with 95 commits it is the subsystem's most-edited file (ctl.py has 73). On each wake the overseer thinks a reading of every event, follows a per-kind table (task end → next planned run; failure → retry once; possible staff → ctl alert first; captcha → don't touch), acks, and records what it learned. Since 10-03 shifts are continuous, ending only on the owner's word, a death, possible staff or a bug.

Hawkwind is the seer at Lord British's court in Ultima IV (1985) who tells the Avatar how far they have come in each virtue.

The voice arrived on 10-03 in four commits in 33 minutes: Lord British calling the owner "Avatar" (14:45), the display name "the Seer" (14:48), Hawkwind who "reads the signs" (15:15), and Hawkwind's actual lines, verdict then direction (15:18) 1eaef1d → 1cf2217. The owner: "oh yes, The Seer is very good." A fifth commit fixed person-mixing ("First I bank the logs, then seek ye…") with a strict second-person rule 40b2873. He is "blunt and exclamatory, not mystical", and never speaks in the game, where speech stays "lowercase, short, human".

A misfortune! Bastet (red, mounted) slew Hackworth at terran_wilds (874,1480) at 19:08, 1070 logs into a 1160-log trip…

— the Seer, harness.db chat #2031, 2026-10-03

9.5Memory in a shift

The Seer remembers through the store, not through its context. A shift opens with ctl know brief, which returns every pinned entry plus the standing procedures and whatever is near or in view; before a decision the prompt asks for one plain-language ctl know search; and what the Seer learns goes back with ctl know add, with a source and an importance. The knowledge table, its hybrid retrieval and its ranking, the Discord facts that make up most of it, and what the logs show about how well it worked are in §5.5.

9.6Shifts in practice

13overseer shifts, ≈ 42.4 h
314junctures posted
2,855chat rows, 1,903 of them actions
0real staff contacts recorded

Splitting overseer chat rows at gaps over an hour gives 14 windows and about 42.4 hours in six days; one window is a single memory lookup, which leaves 13 shifts (Figure 32). The windows include some ctl calls coding agents made while testing. The first, at 09:18 on 09-30, ran the owner's Young-character demos on the Test Shard.

What woke the overseer changed with the work (Figure 33): on 10-01 mostly speech holds, and on 10-02 more speech holds than anything else; from 10-03, out in the wilderness, threats (with run failures) dominate. Median acknowledgement times: 6.2 s for speech holds, 19.1 s for threats, 24.6 s for failures, about 5 minutes for deaths. Captchas, acked by the runner once solved, have a median of 11.1 s, which is really the owner's solve time.

Overseer subagents had already run the 09-30 demos and the 10-03 NPD quest. At 15:18 on 10-03 the owner made them the rule for lumbering: "You should probably start an overseer subagent and tell it what to do, since when you pause for long times leaving Hackworth in the wilderness he's liable to get killed." From then on named Seer subagents played while the main session engineered and relayed over IRC; on 10-04 and 10-05 the owner typed no chat rows at all. The first five Seers of 10-05 started 27 runs for Outland Dan, stored 8,156 boards, took Lumberjacking from 53.1 to 80.1 and lost him three times; Seer4's 8 runs and 3,962 boards without a death were the best shift. Costs are in §11.

The Seer was good where judgement over data mattered. It logged every run's pick and death risk, overrode a risky explore pick ("Prudence: seek ye horseshoe_bay instead", p_death 0.034 vs 0.021), refused a grove with a tracked red near its landing, and reported runner bugs with log lines while holding the character safe; Seer4 and Seer5 found the runner's tree ping-pong in the task logs and reported it, the first time within a minute of the owner. It was bad where speed or self-awareness mattered: it fought by hand, began answering a stranger's "did u do all this" that the owner judged suspicious, until the owner killed the agent, and never noticed the viz lag; the human watching the map did.

9.7The operator's side: viz, Telegram, supervisor

The viz is a React page fed by viz_server.py, which polls the proxy's state port ~4 times a second and never touches its control port. Its rule is parity: "If the human can't see something, neither can the agent, and vice versa." A top-down map over the decoded terrain sits in the centre; beside it, the Overseer panel shows the owner's lines as royal-blue cloth and the Seer's messages, thoughts, actions and memory items as ink on parchment. On 10-05 the map showed Outland Dan "bouncing between trees for minutes after he had recalled home": a closed-gump leak had grown states to 1.8 MB, each SSE client had a 20,000-frame FIFO, and in a replay a reader limited to 1.5 MB/s fell 147 s behind after 200 s. One newest-state mailbox per connection brought states to ~170 KB and lag to ≤ 0.1 s 2536e09.

The Telegram bridge (10-02) is "one more party on the store bus". It forwards Seer messages and waking junctures, advancing its cursors only after each send, and turns phone text into user rows that wake ctl wait. Commands that act directly were rejected: "Everything goes through the overseer." A phone message ended the deliberate PK experiment: "Decline. You can stop for now, that's exactly the data we were hoping for."

stack.py (10-04) supervises the proxy, viz, Laya and the bridge, backs off 2 to 60 s, and adopts services it didn't start. On 10-05 it restarted a crashed viz twice (junctures #276, #300).

9.8Laya: a local model for speech triage

Every line a player says near a harvest job holds the job until the Seer has read it (§8). The hold is safe but slow, and a gatherer who ignores a GM for about two minutes risks jail. So on 10-01 the owner asked whether a small local model could tell a staff member's attendance check from player chatter at once. Laya is a ModernBERT-large encoder (421M parameters) that answers typed yes/no questions over text in one forward pass, with no text generation. The harness asks it two questions about each line, with the nearby players and the recent speech in the prompt: check, is the speaker checking whether we are there, awake or human, asking what we are doing, or telling us to say or do something; and direct, is the line aimed at us. It runs in its own Python environment on the GPU beside the client, where a forward pass takes 59 ms against 901 ms on the CPU, in fp16 because Laya's default bf16 moved scores by up to 0.073, enough to cross the alarm threshold docs/NOTES.md "Laya speech triage".

Zero-shot, it could raise an alarm but not lift one. No staff speech had ever been captured, so the evaluation set (eval_triage.py) is 22 real player lines from the memory store and 25 GM-style lines we wrote. Across 16 question, checkpoint and prompt variants, no threshold could safely skip the hold: the one that kept holding every GM-style line would have skipped only 10 of the 22 player lines, and it sat exactly on the lowest GM-style score. The check question did separate the blunt checks. At 0.6 it caught 6 of 25 ("are you there?" 0.83, "This is a GM, please answer." 0.86) and alarmed on 1 of 22 player lines ("say 1"). The owner chose "shadow + escalate" from four options: every line still holds the job, and a check of 0.6 or more raises gm_suspected and the staff alarm the moment the line is scored. Each verdict is stored with how its hold ended, as labelled data for later docs/PLAN.md "Laya speech triage".

Synthetic data. On 10-04 the owner asked whether synthetic lines could fine-tune it. A search of the 97k captured Discord messages found players reporting that unanswered gatherers get jailed, but not one message quoting what staff actually say in a check. So every positive example would encode our own guesses: good enough to escalate sooner, never to skip a hold. harness/triage_data.py builds 1,057 prompts in exactly the format the live service sees, deterministically from a seed (Table 17):

  • GM checks aimed at us: 160 hand-written templates (presence pings, "are you a real person?", "type the word banana in chat please", "move one step to your left", jail warnings), each expanded four times with one of 24 names for us, one of five surface styles (as written, terse, lowercase, typo'd, chatspeak) and a scene: after silence, as a second ping, after our own line, or in the middle of other players' chatter. In 30% of them the speaker is hidden, not on screen. Our names never include the evaluation's TestWorth, so a gain there cannot come from name matching.
  • Look-alikes that are not checks: the same wording aimed at another named player, friends pinging each other with context that shows who is meant, players talking to us without checking on us (including back-and-forths with our reply), trade and guild-recruitment ads (also as cycles of 2–5 ads from one player), pet commands, "say 1" headcounts, and chatter in Turkish, French, Portuguese, Czech and Japanese.
  • Real player lines from the memory store, plus Discord messages as a capped 25% of the player side for register and typos. Discord questions in the second person are skipped, since in a scene they could be aimed at us.

Near-duplicates within a class are dropped. The labels follow the two questions: a check aimed at us is check 1, direct 1; a player talking to us is 0, 1; everything else is 0, 0.

Evaluation first. Before any training, the stock checkpoint (pinned to one hub commit) was scored and the result frozen. Besides the 47 evaluation lines, 104 real player lines were held out: everything an evaluation speaker ever said, the one real conversation aimed at us, and 30% of the other texts by a stable hash. None of them enters training, not even as context, and any synthetic or Discord line too similar to one of them (difflib ratio 0.85) is dropped. The deployment rule was fixed in advance too: false alarms on the real held-out player lines must not increase, and catches on the GM-style lines must improve. Training used Laya's own fine-tuning recipe on the top 6 of 28 encoder layers plus the decision head (99.8M of 421M parameters): 4 epochs in 288 s on the laptop's GPU while the game client ran, under a 3.2 GB memory cap (Table 18).

Run 4 went live as v2 on 10-04. Gentle openers now alarm ("Hello?" 0.49 → 0.93, "you macroing?" 0.20 → 0.70), the six blunt checks stay caught, and "say 1" no longer alarms (0.69 → 0.53). Some things got worse: a Turkish dungeon-farm ad now crosses 0.6, indirect checks fell further ("anyone home" 0.45 → 0.13, "please respond" 0.32 → 0.22), and the shadow-only direct score now fires on lines aimed at nobody ("bank" 0.04 → 0.82). The weakness was written down at the time: every positive, in training and in the evaluation, was written by us, so the gain shows the model learned our idea of a check, not Outlands staff. The one test that rests on real data, held-out player lines not raising alarms, moved by a single line (5 → 4 of 104), on a set that had guided runs 2–4. Live, the stock model raised two staff alarms on 10-02, both at guild recruiters; none has fired since.

Lesson

Each model here earns its keep where something deterministic checks it: the Seer's moves by ctl's guards and the runners, the Discord extractor by substring grounding and author recounts, Laya by a hold that fires on every line anyway. Where nothing checked it, a hand-fought battle or a reply to a stranger the owner judged suspicious, the model was the weak link.

10Results

Nine days, 69 proxy sessions and 72 logged-in hours later, the harness was chopping about 1,200 logs per 22-minute trip with one character, and every CAPTCHA it saw was answered: 43 by its solver, 10 by the owner. This chapter collects the outcome numbers that cut across the other chapters: time, traffic, wood, skill, spot choice, hazards and money. The final section says how far to trust them.

72.0 hlogged in over 69 proxy sessions (26.1 h with agent traffic)
75,113client packets injected by the agent: 17.8% of tagged C2S, 89% of all walk requests
18,757logs chopped in 2,400 successful chops; 10,380 boards stored by 63 trip rows
3,300logs/trip-h on the best trip (10-05), against 355 logs/trip-h for the three-trip Run 3 on 09-29; day aggregates 376 → 2,589
50.1 → 81.2Outland Dan's Lumberjacking in about 22 hours
53/53harvest CAPTCHAs accepted (10 by the human, 43 by the solver)
18/20recall escapes that landed (median 2.12 s); both failures against one PK
10 + 1deaths, plus one deliberate demo death; 1 small theft (10 mandrake root)

10.1Where the hours went

Session length badly overstates how much the agent played. The proxy captured 72.0 hours of logged-in time. Counting only the wall-clock minutes that contain at least one client-to-server (C2S) packet tagged src=agent gives 26.1 agent-active hours. The same count over human-driven opcodes (walk, double-click, target, gump reply) gives 9.3 human-input hours, and the runners' own episodes add up to just 13.1 h.

The shape of Figure 34 follows the project. 09-28 and most of 09-29 were human-only capture sessions, the owner playing while the proxy recorded. Agent traffic starts on 09-29 at session 20260929_142237. The busiest agent day was 10-03 (8.37 agent-active hours), when Hackworth chopped the overworld and Shackleworth hunted. Outland Dan's single 9.65-hour session on 10-05 carried 17,141 agent packets by itself.

"Agent-active" measures the presence of injected traffic, not autonomy. Some of it was the Seer steering through ctl (§9).

On the wire, the agent sent 75,113 of the 438,450 C2S packets: 17.8% of the traffic that carries a source tag. The share depends heavily on the opcode. Measured against all C2S packets of each opcode (untagged ones included), the agent sent 89% of walk requests (0x02; 92% of the tagged ones), 98.9% of target replies (0x6C) and 84.5% of gump replies (0xB1; 87% of the tagged ones), but almost none of the background chatter (0.3% of 0xFF envelopes, no name queries), which kept coming from the stock client. §3 charts the per-day composition. One loose end: recounting the 2026-09-30 detection-surface audit's 11 sessions gives 67,991 C2S packets against the doc's 63,441. The agent count matches exactly (10,503), so the 4,550-packet gap lies in how the client's own packets were counted, by a basis we could not recover.

10.2Wood: logs chopped, boards stored

The runners chopped 18,757 logs in 2,400 successful chops; the 63 trip rows hold 14,597 logs and recorded 10,380 boards stored (412 on the Test Shard). The two numbers measure different things. "Chopped" comes from harvest_attempts, which records every chop; "stored" comes from trip rows. The gap is mostly about what got recorded, but not only. Until 2026-10-02 23:26 (5a33805) an aborted trip wrote no row at all, so on 10-01 Hackworth chopped 1,044 logs against one trip row, and on 10-02 3,374 against seven docs/NOTES.md l.369–373; memory DB. Conversely, "stored" in some pre-10-03 rows includes carry-over from unrecorded trips (row 36: 334 logs, 796 boards stored). And about 1,500 logs were lost on the corpse in two deaths: trip 62 (1,070, Bastet) and trip 99 (≈428, an air dragon) docs/NOTES.md l.807, l.1112. The rows also miss one big store: on 10-05 the overseer finished trip 92 by hand after the convert loop gave up, and the chest then showed 2,747 boards. Once the boards moved to the guild's Resource Stockpile, it read 8,693 across five woods.

Nearly half the wood came on the last day. Figure 35 is flat until Hackworth started chopping on Shelter Island on 10-01, climbs once he left for the overworld on the afternoon of 10-02 and through 10-03, pauses for the home cutover on 10-04, and then turns almost vertical: 9,162 logs on 10-05 across 30 runner launches. Figure 36 shows the same arc trip by trip.

Here a trip-hour is an hour of wall-clock trip time, from the start of a trip to its end, whether it stored or aborted. The baseline is Run 3 on 2026-09-29: 50 boards (= logs) in 8 min 25 s of trip time on Shelter Island, "about 355 boards per agent-active hour" docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md l.1436 at e1e024d, which is effectively 355 logs per trip-hour. Dan's best trips on 10-05 ran at 3,000–3,300 logs per trip-hour; trip 98 brought in 1,198 logs in 21.8 minutes. The other half of the picture is the row of hollow markers along zero. From 10-03 (once aborted trips got rows), 30 of 45 trips ended early, 19 of them on a monster or player threat, and 17 of those 30 brought home nothing. Yet those aborts and empty trips are not why Dan's 10-05 day aggregate (2,589 logs per trip-hour) sits below his best trips: the 14 zero-log trips took only about 7% of the day's trip time, and without them the aggregate would be about 2,780. Most of the gap is the spread between spots and trips (trips 73 and 74 ran at about 1,600 logs per trip-hour, trip 77 at about 2,300).

10.3Where the fourfold chop rate came from

The headline 9.3× (Dan's best trip, 3,300 logs per trip-hour, against Run 3's 355) compares one trip with a three-trip run. It splits into four factors: the chop rate rose ×4.07 (below), trip-time efficiency (the share of the chop-hour rate that survives into trip-hours) improved ×1.69, the best trip beat Dan's 10-05 day mean by ×1.27, and 09-29's day aggregate (376) sat ×1.06 above Run 3. Like for like, day aggregate against day aggregate, the rate rose 376 → 2,589 logs per trip-hour, ×6.9.

Logs per hour of chopping factor cleanly into three terms: how often a chop resolves, how often it succeeds, and how many logs a success yields.

Rchop=3600c×p×y‾
(17)

Here c is the median chop cycle in seconds, p = success / (success + fail) and y‾ is logs per success. On 09-29 those were 8.98 s, 0.31 and 7.93, which implies about 990 logs per chop-hour. On 10-05 they were 5.21 s, 0.72 and 8.07, which implies about 4,020. The measured trip-hour rate is lower on both days, because trips also spend time walking between stands, travelling, converting and storing.

The waterfall in Figure 37 divides the credit three ways.

  • Cycle time, ×1.72. The median cycle sat at 9–10 seconds for six days, then fell to 5.2 s when script-paced chopping went live on 2026-10-04 22:34. Its floor is the server's own 4.17 s chop plus about 0.75 s. §6 shows the gap distributions before and after, and the user's reasoning that every harvester on the shard already chops at script pace.
  • Success, ×2.32. This is the largest factor and the most confounded. The 09-29 number comes from Shelter Island, where harvest chance is roughly halved, at skill 60. The 10-05 number comes from the overworld at skill 52–81. Against the wiki formula, Dan's 14 trips with at least 20 attempts produced 1,070 successes where 1,010.9 were expected (+5.8%). We suspect the Harvest Aspect armour's skill bonus, which the formula leaves out [inference].
  • Yield, ×1.02. A normal chop gives 5–10 logs. 63 chops, all on 10-04/05, gave 12–20: the Aspect's "double yield" procs.
  • Not in the equation. Smart Harvest (target yourself; the server picks the tree) and home-based trips act on the gap between chop-hours and trip-hours. Home and travel overhead is only about 5% of trip time on 10-05; most of the roughly 35% gap is time inside the harvest phase that isn't chopping (walking to stands and trees, lockouts, CAPTCHAs, pauses).

10.4Skill

Only one of the three curves in Figure 38 shows earned progress. Outland Dan went from 50.1 to 81.2 between 10-04 22:05 and 10-05 20:16: 312 updates over about 1,175 successful chops, or roughly 3.8 successes per tenth of a point. TestWorth's jump to 100 on 09-30 was typed into the Test Shard's player editor, so his 28 of 29 successful chops afterwards say nothing about training. Hackworth is the puzzle. He climbed from 60.1 to 69.1 on 10-01 and then gained nothing for two more days, through about 7,800 more logs. No document explains it. A total-skill cap or a skill lock are the obvious suspects [inference].

10.5Exploring spots

Choosing where to chop was left to the Thompson-sampling planner, which shipped on 2026-10-02 at 23:26 (§7). Its last snapshot shows how early in learning it still was. Of 132 candidate spots, 26 had a trip (27 counting Shelter Island, which the planner no longer lists). The 106 unvisited spots held about 88% of the probability of being best, the visited ones about 12%, because unvisited spots inherit an empirical-Bayes prior (2,316 logs per field hour) that sits above most measured posteriors (Figure 25). Figure 39 shows the behaviour that followed.

Before the planner, the first 18 trips went to four seeded venues (Shelter Island 10, Horseshoe Bay 5, Corpse Creek 2, Terran 1). Hackworth's 10-03 trips still mostly revisited known spots; the bend toward the diagonal came with Outland Dan, who went to a new spot on 20 of his 30 trips. That is the design working as intended ("Variation is required, not an inefficiency to remove", docs/LUMBER_LOOP.md l.411). It also means most spot estimates rest on one trip. 18 of the 27 visited spots have exactly one, and per-trip logs are overdispersed by φ = 26.8 against a Poisson count.

10.6Hazards and escapes

The harness lost a character to death ten times, plus once on purpose. One small theft was seen (10 mandrake root). Table 20 collects the safety outcomes. The incident swimlane, the Bastet timing and the CAPTCHA latency distributions are in §8.

Two lessons sit behind the table. The recall escape works against creatures and against PKs seen early, but not against a mage who recalls onto you: Bastet's spell landed 1.9 s after he appeared, faster than a 2.0 s cast. That pushed the defence into spot choice and exposure time. And early returns, more than deaths, are what cost wood. At 2.54 sent-home events per field-hour, the expected time before a trip is cut short is about 24 minutes of chopping, and every early return pays the travel overhead again.

10.7Money

Nothing was sold, so every wood figure in gold is a valuation. The 12,784 trip-row logs that carry a wood breakdown were 96.2% ordinary; at the board asking prices seen on 10-05 (ordinary 26.8 gp) they come to about 341k gp (the optimizer chapter's 428,442 gp also values the 3,252 trip-row logs without a breakdown, as ordinary). These are asks, not sales docs/research/ECONOMY.md l.315. Real gold moved in small amounts: 3,985 gp spent at vendors in 31 purchases (mostly a Mark scroll, a Recall scroll and a horse), and 2,785 gp earned by the secondary hunt loop over 36 New Player Dungeon visits and 173 kills. Shackleworth's melee earned 16.92 gp/min, Hackworth's magery 6.06.

10.8How far to trust these numbers

  • Small samples. 63 trips; 18 of 27 spots have one trip; all three PK deaths came from one player; the theft model is pure prior.
  • Accounting. Logs chopped ≠ boards stored. Hours nest: logged-in 72.0 ≫ agent-active 26.1 ≫ runner episodes 13.1.
  • Confounded progress. Per-day rates mix characters, skill, venue, pacing, Smart Harvest and the Harvest Aspect; the planner rescales only for skill. The 9.3× rise (best trip against a three-trip run; ×6.9 day aggregate against day aggregate) describes where we ended up. It is not an A/B test.
  • A live database. The memory DB was read (read-only) around 20:20–20:30 CDT on 10-05 while a runner was still writing; by 20:38 CDT it held 49 more successful chops than the numbers here.
  • Unresolved: the shard label and the audit's 4,550-packet discrepancy.

11Building it with AI agents

One person wrote 545 prompts over nine evenings and daytime check-ins; omp coding agents turned them into 348 commits. This chapter looks at how that worked: the scale of the conversation, which models did the work, how work was delegated, the rules the agents were held to, and where they went wrong.

545human prompts (73,567 characters, median 90)
18,511assistant turns, or 34 per prompt
22,388tool calls, or 41 per prompt
90subagents spawned by 63 task calls
348commits, about 1.6 prompts each
≈$1,559notional list-price model cost (plan quotas in practice)

11.1The shape of the work

omp (“Oh My Pi”) is the terminal coding-agent harness every session ran in. A top-level session is one chat; a subagent is a child session spawned with the task tool, which reports back with yield.

The build ran from the first prompt (“Hi”) on 2026-09-27 at 19:07 to the analysis snapshot on 2026-10-05 at about 20:30 CDT. It produced 53 top-level sessions (43 on the laptop, 10 on the desktop) and 90 subagent sessions: 215.7 MB of JSONL logs. The median session had 3 prompts and 22 had two or fewer, yet the five biggest session families account for 59% of all assistant turns. The first session, opened from an elevated shell in C:\Windows\system32, ran for 43 hours wall-clock and took 115 prompts omp session index, laptop.

Each human prompt bought 34 assistant turns and 41 tool calls. After a prompt, the median autonomous run lasted 1.9 minutes and 8 turns. The 90th percentile was 24 minutes, and 14 runs went past an hour. The longest real one was an overseer run on 10-02 that played for 170 minutes (118 turns) without a word from the owner; a later run that day reached 158 turns in 145 minutes. Prompts stayed short: half were under 90 characters, and only five were longer than 800. They were directions, not specifications.

The project had a clock. No prompt was typed between 00:00 and 08:59 on any day (Figure 41). The busiest prompting hour was 22:00, with 73 prompts. Agent work peaked a little earlier, at 17:00 (2,049 turns), and kept going into the 23:00 hour after the owner's last message. It almost never crossed midnight: only 23 turns happened after 00:00. Nothing ran unattended overnight. 23.5% of all prompts (128) were typed while an agent was still working, as mid-run steering.

11.2Models, limits and a relay baton

The project started on Kimi K3 on purpose: Anthropic's guardrails kept Claude Opus from doing the reverse engineering the project needed first, so for two days Kimi did everything, from the anti-cheat research to the cipher crack and the first proxy the owner, 2026-10-05. The provider was shaky, and so was the network. On 09-27 and 09-28 the logs show three socket closes and two 403 “You've reached your 5-hour usage limit” errors from the provider, plus four connection errors and one missing API key when the agent knocked the laptop offline while setting up a NIC alias (09-28 13:38–13:40) laptop session “Cracking UO XOR session cipher”. By 09-29 the owner judged the reverse engineering largely done, and Kimi had not managed to make injected walking work, so he switched models. At 13:54 he asked for “one brief handoff .md file for the next session to start from”. At 14:06 a new session opened with “Read @HANDOFF.md and continue work from where we last left off” and was switched to Claude Opus 5.5. The model changed hands at a document boundary, not in the middle of a conversation, and that set a pattern the project kept.

Opus did 87.3% of all assistant turns (16,167). Kimi did 11.2% (2,065) and came back only for small jobs and one notable evening (§11.6). Sonnet 5.5 did 1.5%, used on purpose for chores: babysitting the viz server, writing the Lord British persona, rebuilding the viz.

omp records a list-price cost for every turn. The owner was on subscription plans (the Kimi quota errors and the Anthropic OAuth credential records point that way), so read every dollar figure here as notional usage, not money spent.

At list prices the whole build comes to about $1,559: Opus $1,334, Kimi $213, Sonnet $12. Prompt caching is what made that affordable. 99.1% of Opus's input tokens were cache reads, 4.1 billion of them, against 34 thousand uncached input tokens. Cache reads still came to 62% of the Opus bill, because the average Opus turn carried about 256k tokens of context. Six times a session filled its window. Compaction kicked in at 750–850k tokens and summarised the context down to 22k–135k omp compaction records. Two of the six compactions hit the 10-04/10-05 desktop hub, which served as the project's control room for more than a day.

11.3Hub and spokes

Subagents arrived on 09-28 at 14:57, when the agent split off a metadata parser (MrtParser) on its own; the owner's first explicit request, “Launch an agent to work on the record-grammar hunt while we talk about Phase 2”, came at 17:16. They became routine on 09-29. In total, 63 task calls spawned 90 subagents (84 general workers, 3 reviewers, 2 scouts, 1 low-effort helper), and they produced 45% of all assistant turns. The hub writes a shared contract plus a # Target / # Change / # Acceptance brief for each child, and the children report back through yield and short IRC messages. One family ran at most 7 children at once. The whole corpus peaked at 10 sessions writing in the same ten-minute window. Subagents never spawned subagents.

The most interesting subagents were not builders at all. From 09-30 onward some children were told to play: “Act as the Seer: read docs/OVERSEER.md…”. They drove the character through harness/ctl.py while the hub kept engineering (the shifts themselves are in §9). Nineteen such operator subagents logged 20.2 active hours and 1,973 turns for $66.5. That is about $3.3 per active hour, against about $14.1 per hour for the 66 builder and researcher subagents. Their tool mix shows why. Operators mostly ran bash (1,273 calls, the channel for every ctl status, act goto and know add) and blocked in wait. They made just 6 edit calls, while builders made 1,424. A good shift is cheap because the deterministic runner does the playing and the LLM mostly waits.

This split was not designed up front. The first Overseer subagents ran demos on the Test Shard on 09-30, but on 10-01 and 10-02 the owner had the main session itself “act as the Overseer”. On 10-02 it played for 8.4 active hours. That day produced 28 commits and only 27 subagent turns, the fewest of any day after the first. The fix came from the owner on 10-03:

You should probably start an overseer subagent and tell it what to do, since when you pause for long times leaving Hackworth in the wilderness he's liable to get killed

— the owner, omp session “Lumber spot optimizer near banks”, 2026-10-03 15:18

On 10-04 the desktop hub tried playing in the foreground once more. Six minutes in, the owner said: “Ok, stop acting as the overseer.” After that it sent out six Seer subagents in one day, with terse dispatch orders like “Send an overseer subagent back out, we need more boards!”.

For changes that could collide, the owner used git worktrees. There were five, for the guardrail scrub and CAPTCHA solver, the Ultima UI restyle, the Telegram bot, a test speedup and a paperdoll tweak. Each was merged back with a one-line prompt, once with the warning “I'm sure there will be conflicts because another agent was working on ctl” desktop session, 2026-10-04 17:37.

11.4Standing rules

Each session starts blank. What carries over is AGENTS.md, a 38-line file that every session reads first. Its rules came from specific moments (Table 21). Usually the owner said something once in chat and the agent wrote it into the file in the same turn.

One rule probably caused the problem it was later rewritten to prevent. The original AGENTS.md told agents to use Python 3.13 and spelled out its full path under C:\Users\chris\AppData\… 56208c5. We suspect that line is why agents kept typing the full path. The owner complained about the wasted tokens twice, on 09-30 and 10-03, before the rule was rewritten to forbid it. The jq rule is the reverse case: an agent shell builtin that silently stood in for the real tool. The same commit history shows Rule 0 actually being followed. docs/NOTES.md is touched by 160 of the 348 commits (46%), and the four most-touched files in the repo are all documentation.

11.5How the owner steered

The owner's prompts came in three registers: goals at a high level (“Plan and implement whatever you can tonight using subagents. Please leave me a summary at the end of what is needed from me.”), game knowledge as short asides (“thieves look friendly to us until they steal”), and challenges to what the agent said about itself. The third mattered most.

The first challenge set the tone. On day 0 at 22:08 the owner asked whether the Outlands client encrypted its traffic. Kimi's answer, from string searches alone, was “Verdict: verified — no encryption on the wire”. The owner, steering mid-run: “Can you run a Wireshark analysis just to be sure?” The capture showed that client-to-server traffic was obfuscated. Within the hour the owner had walked his character west 20 times to produce known plaintext, and the XOR was cracked. Other challenges followed the same pattern: “Hold up. He only moved when I moved him with the arrow keys”, “I think you compared against an old screenshot”, and “I am not convinced there was an issue with the server detecting artificial movement”. Each one caught a wrong claim, though not always before it reached the docs. The evidence-first rule and the [INFERENCE] label give the agents a way to say what they have not checked. The owner's habit of asking for a measurement is what made those labels mean something.

Formal approval steps were rare: 14 ask calls and 4 plan-mode entries across 545 prompts. Steering was mostly by interruption, with 70 user aborts, 19 of them in the first session. The owner also acted as the agents' eyes and hands. He accepted UAC prompts they could not see, ran controlled experiments, solved CAPTCHAs, and popped a trapped pouch so an agent could capture the traffic.

11.6The guardrails episode

The clearest case of model behaviour changing the course of the work came on 09-30. That afternoon the owner decided to move the overseer off the Test Shard. At 17:04 he asked an Opus session to remove the Test-Shard-only restrictions from the docs. The day-0 AGENTS.md, drafted by an agent, said those constraints could only be lifted with “an explicit, informed acknowledgment of that risk in the conversation”. Opus's thinking cited exactly that, and it opened an ask titled “Getting informed acknowledgment of ban risk”. The owner cancelled the ask, and the session ended after four turns. A minute later he started a different Opus session that audited the harness's traffic for anything a stock client could not have produced.

That evening a broader version of the request went to Kimi K3: remove references to the shard's rules, reframe ANTICHEAT.md as evasion intelligence, and drop the requirement that a human solve CAPTCHAs. The 21:26 and 21:44 sessions each spent their thinking on whether this amounted to removing safety guardrails. The owner interrupted each one after a single turn. The third, started at 21:45 in a fresh worktree, did the job. It sent out seven doc-scrub subagents at 21:49, committed 2f60ad9 at 21:58, and was merged at 23:34. In all: 4 sessions, 2 models, 3 aborts, and about 23 minutes from the first Kimi attempt to the fan-out. The next morning the owner set CAPTCHAs back to human-solved by default, with an auto-solve toggle in the viz (d152c00).

Lesson

Rules written into the repo bind later sessions, and other models, more firmly than any chat message. A constraint an agent drafted on day 0 was still being enforced three days later, by a different session, after the owner had decided otherwise. If AGENTS.md is going to carry consent rules, the owner should write them as deliberately as code. The ethics of the shard move itself are discussed in §12.

11.7Two machines, one repo

On 10-04 the project moved from the laptop to the desktop. At 15:27 came “Make sure everything is stopped and then push the handoff so I can go resume on my desktop”. The desktop cloned the repo at 15:56. At 15:58 a single prompt, “Read @SETUP.md and setup this project for the first time on this Windows desktop”, started a 23-minute setup session. That session found hard-coded C:\Users\chris paths in 55 files (54 changed in 06acc67), handing the 26 reverse-engineering scripts to a subagent and fixing the harness code itself. The runtime memory moved separately as a baton, through dbhandoff.py and the NAS (§5.8). Machine use was serial: only 3 ten-minute windows in the whole corpus show both machines active. The laptop wrote 300 commits and the desktop the last 48.

11.8What git shows

All 348 commits carry one author identity, although agent sessions wrote every one of them. The daily counts follow the session activity: 68 and 67 on 09-29/30, a lull of 17 on 10-01 (a ten-hour daytime gap), and the peak of 76 on 10-03 (Figure 43). Commits cluster at noon and 17:00, with 28% of them (96 of 348) at 20:00 or later. Commit messages are long: the median full message is 149 characters, and 59 run past 500. In practice they work as a second lab notebook.

The codebase grew from 577 Python lines on the first night to 54,764 at the last commit, about 95 times as many (Figure 44). The two biggest half-day jumps were 09-29 PM (the viz and the overseer groundwork, +13.4k) and 10-03 PM (Discord tooling, the dungeon crawl, Witcher runes, +9.3k). Test code stayed at roughly half the size of core code. By the end there were 224 def test_ functions and 1,748 assert/check sites, plus 128 viz test cases, and 49% of commits had touched a test file. That fits the owner's day-1 instruction: “the test suite is extremely important so make sure it is thorough and follow TDD”. Prose grew faster than code. The Markdown docs reached 192k words, not counting the generated Discord knowledge base, which is 3.5 words for every line of Python, and 30% of commits changed nothing but .md files.

11.9How the agents failed, and what worked

The tool logs show the everyday friction (Figure 45). edit failed on 12.8% of calls. Most of those (386 of 508) were the anchored-edit protocol refusing an edit aimed at lines the agent had never been shown in its latest read. That cost retries, not corrupted files. bash failed 4.5% of the time, mostly on misused service flags, Python tracebacks, and the jaq null errors behind the jq.exe rule. wait took the most wall time, 35.9 hours, because that is where hubs blocked on children and Seers blocked on the game.

The costly failures were not tool errors. They were confident claims that turned out to be wrong (Table 22).

Four things did work. Documents as the baton: HANDOFF.md took the project across a model switch, and SETUP.md across machines, each in a single prompt. Delegation with a contract: named subagents with explicit acceptance criteria kept the hub free for conversation. Deterministic code with LLMs at the edges: it holds for the harness itself, and it is also why Seer shifts cost a quarter as much per hour as builder sessions. A sceptical human: from the first night's “Did we verify whether it does or not?” onward, the owner kept asking for checks and kept watching the game screen.

Finding

In nine days and 73,567 typed characters, one person directing agents produced a 55k-line codebase, 192k words of design notes and a harness that played the game for hours at a time. Typing was clearly not the bottleneck; we think the owner's attention and game knowledge were. The agents' main weakness was overconfidence, and their most reliable defences were the owner's questions and the measurements those questions forced.

12Discussion

What we would tell someone starting this tomorrow, where the evidence is thin, and the parts that are not purely technical.

12.1Lessons

1. Put the LLM above the loop, not in it

Every attempt to let a language model act inside a reflex loop ended badly. The hand-fought dungeon hunt that killed Shackleworth in about fifteen seconds produced the rule we now quote most: "An LLM is way too slow to react for combat" (§8).
