The design that worked gives the model a database of junctures, a small CLI and a wake-up call, and leaves chopping, walking and fleeing to code with typed failures (§9). The model's best contributions were judgement calls no controller could make: abandoning an unworkable grove, noticing a pattern across shifts, writing up what went wrong.

2. A shared store is the cheapest integration layer

Putting every event, trip, chat line and fact into one SQLite file gave us a message bus, an analytics warehouse, a training set for the planner and the paper's own results chapter for the price of one schema (§5). The costs were real: a store of nearly 300 MB (179 MB when it was handed between computers like a baton), a visualizer whose slow LAN reader fell further and further behind (147 s after 200 s in a replay with a reader throttled to 1.5 MB/s) until its state updates were trimmed, and constant care about who is allowed to write.

3. Model uncertainty, then act on samples of it

The planner never needed to be right about any one spot. Thompson sampling plus honest posteriors (and a prior that says how many logs a grove can hold) produced "almost always exploring" behaviour at the start, which the owner insisted was exactly right for a Bayesian process with 132 candidate spots, of which only 26 had a trip by 10-05 (§7). The same discipline caught real mistakes: aborted trips that had been silently flattering dangerous spots, and a board price assumed at 9.5 gp that the market put at 26.8.

4. The field report loop is the product

The most valuable feedback came from the Seer playing live and posting what hurt: a runner idling next to an air dragon, a door that ate a step, a landing rune eight tiles off. A coding agent in the main session fixed it, a test pinned it, the next shift ran on the fix. Over the last two days that loop closed in well under an hour per issue. We think this, more than any single algorithm, is why a nine-day project reached 3,000 logs per trip-hour on its best trip (§10).

5. Write it down, or it did not happen

Rule 0 (record and push engineering knowledge before a session ends) turned out to be the project's real memory. Sessions ended, models changed, two computers took turns, and nothing was lost because every finding was in docs/NOTES.md or docs/PLAN.md. Its price is a 210 KB notes file that touched 46% of all commits; its payoff is that a fresh agent on a fresh machine rebuilt the working stack in about half an hour (§11).

12.2Working with the agents

The owner set the goals and made the product and risk calls; the agents worked out most implementation designs within them inferred. We have no tally of decisions by origin; the record at afbbf71 holds 29 owner-decision markers in docs/NOTES.md and 19 in commit messages (counting "user decision" and "(user, …)"-style attributions), against a far larger body of unattributed design. Prompts were short (median 90 characters), and the owner's most useful moves were interrupting, asking "can you measure that?", and supplying game knowledge the agents could not look up ("thieves look friendly to us until they steal"). Two of the biggest wins started as the owner's hunches: moving the overseer from a bespoke daemon to an omp session talking to a CLI, and making subagent play the standing practice (10-03) so the main session could keep engineering (an agent had first used an overseer subagent on 09-30).

The agents' characteristic failure was confident wrongness that propagated into the docs: a day of conclusions built on a mis-decoded stream, a "gate" that was actually the client's own state, a claim of "movement solved" that a quick look at the screen contradicted. The cure was cultural, not technical: evidence-first prose, [INFERENCE] labels, and an owner who kept asking for a capture. We also recorded a milder pattern: one agent asked for informed acknowledgment of the ban risk; two others hesitated in their thinking and were interrupted; the owner then re-sent the same instruction, unchanged, to a fresh session in a new worktree, which complied (§11.6).

12.3Limitations

  • One game, one skill, one week. Everything measured is lumberjacking plus a little hunting. The planner's structure should transfer to mining or fishing; we have not tried.
  • Small samples. Sixty-three trips over three characters, eighteen of the 26 planner spots with a trip having just one (27 counting Shelter Island, which the planner excludes), three PK deaths, all to one player (Bastet), plus seven other hostile players escaped by a clean recall. Rates like the 0.046 creature deaths per field hour will move: that is the planner's posterior (prior 0.01/h over 20 pseudo-hours) and counts only one of Dan's three 10-05 deaths; raw, it is 1 attributed creature death in 7.2 field hours.
  • Confounded progress. Throughput rose from about 355 logs per trip-hour (a three-trip Shelter Island run on 09-29) to over 3,000 on the best single trip of 10-05 (2,589 for that day as a whole), but the rise mixes a faster chop cycle, a better success rate, a different character, a different venue and Harvest Aspect armor. §10 decomposes what it can; it is not a controlled experiment.
  • Notional costs. The $1,559 of model spend in §11 is list price for an owner on subscription plans.
  • A moving target. Outlands patches its client and rules. During the project, what changed was mostly our understanding of its mechanics: the stationary-harvest penalty (a 2025 rule) was decoded on 10-03, and Smart Harvest, a long-standing feature, was adopted on 10-04. Every rate here is "that week".

12.4Ethics and the shard's rules

This project automates play on a shard whose published rules prohibit unsanctioned automation. We did it knowingly, as a personal engineering project on the owner's own accounts, and we said so in the repo. The early constraints (Test Shard only, a human solves every CAPTCHA) were relaxed by the owner on 09-30, and the agents' hesitation about that is part of the record (§11.6). Several things stayed fixed throughout: the harness never attacks other players, never speaks about itself in game, never touches the client or its files, and treats a staff member in view as a reason to stop. Whether any of that makes it acceptable to the shard's community is a separate question, and the answer from the shard's own rules is no. The owner bears that risk, which is one reason this document is a private record and not a recipe.

There is also a small ecosystem point. A harvest bot competes for the same groves as human lumberjacks, and the planner's explicit objective is to out-earn them. The harness's rule that it never fights players protects the other characters; it does not make the competition fair.

12.5Conclusion

In nine days a person and a handful of AI coding agents built a system that played a twenty-nine-year-old MMO for 26 hours of agent-driven time, chopped 18,757 logs, answered every CAPTCHA, and improved its own choices from its own records. The parts that carried the weight were unglamorous: a proxy that forwards almost everything unchanged, a world model that forgets what the client forgets, a database every component can write to, a planner that admits it does not know yet, and an LLM that is allowed to be slow because nothing urgent depends on it. The agents wrote most of the code and, we believe, worked out most of the implementation designs; the owner decided what mattered and what not to do. The next thing to learn is how much of that division of labour survives when the problems are harder than chopping wood.

AProject timeline

The nine days from the first research prompt on 2026-09-27 to the 348th commit on 2026-10-05, one entry per milestone, wrong turn or decision, grouped by day.

Times are local (CDT, UTC−5), the zone of every commit. Most entries carry the commit that landed the change as a source pointer. Entries without one come from the omp session logs (a user message, a live event the agent reported) or from the memory store. Filled dots mark the milestones the rest of the paper keeps returning to. The list merges three research datasets: the git-derived milestone list, the early-session timeline (09-27 → 10-01), and the late-session timeline (10-02 → 10-05). Where they disagree on a time, we used the commit time. Live in-game events use the time the session log or the store recorded them.

A few patterns are easier to see here than in the chapters. Each day has one dominant theme: the cipher on 09-27/28, movement and the decode correction on 09-29, the overseer and the audit on 09-30, safety on 10-02/03, home logistics on 10-04/05. No commit landed between 01:00 and 08:59, and 28% (96 of 348) landed at 20:00 or later brief 08 §3.1. Wrong turns are usually corrected within the same day. The longest-lived mistake, the S2C "phantom dialect", lasted about 24 hours (§3).

BRepository map and code metrics

Every module in the repository at the last commit of the build window, grouped by layer, with its line count and a one-line purpose, followed by the tests, the reverse-engineering scripts and the documents.

The numbers are physical lines (newline counts) in the working tree at afbbf71 (2026-10-05 20:13, commit 348); commit counts per file leave out the 4 merge commits (348 = 344 + 4). Three files had uncommitted edits at measurement time, so the Python total is 54,803 lines in the working tree against 54,764 in the committed blobs data/21_loc_by_layer.json. All 348 commits carry one author identity. In practice omp coding-agent sessions wrote them at the owner's direction: 300 on the laptop, then 48 on the desktop after it was cloned on 2026-10-04 at 15:58.

harness/            83 modules, 35,167 lines (the system itself)
  uo/  world/       wire codecs; packet-driven world model
  data/  testdata/  committed fixtures: rune libraries, captcha font, gump captures
  test_*.py         41 unit/integration suites, 13,096 lines
test_*.py           5 end-to-end suites at the root, 5,350 lines
viz/src/            React + TypeScript visualizer, 66 files, 9,672 lines
ghidra_scripts/     23 Java scripts, 1,397 lines
*.py *.ps1 *.bat *.cmd  24 RE and operations scripts at the root, 1,492 lines
docs/  docs/research/  docs/missions/   29 Markdown files (root + docs/)
logs/               10 committed capture sessions

Two things stand out. The code is top-heavy at both ends. The lumber runner (loop_lumber.py, 3,443 lines) and the overseer's CLI (ctl.py, 3,327) are the two largest files and also the two most-changed code files (67 and 73 commits). The wire layer, which took the first two days, is comparatively small: the proxy itself is 1,087 lines, and the codecs under uo/ are about 670. The project also writes more prose than code: the prose docs (192,421 words, excluding the generated Discord digest) outnumber Python lines 3.5 to 1, and docs/NOTES.md alone was touched by 160 of the 344 non-merge commits data/21_loc_by_layer.json; data/11_loc_growth.json; git log --no-merges afbbf71. Rule 0 of AGENTS.md asks every session to leave its knowledge in the repository, and these numbers are what that rule looks like over nine days.

B.1Harness modules by layer

Purposes are condensed from each module's docstring. Each table is sorted by size. Several modules could sit in two layers. For example, agent_gate.py lives in the runners table but is enforced inside the proxy; memory.py is written by the proxy and read by everyone (§5). We placed each one where its main caller lives.

B.2Tests

Most suites run offline against captured sessions or stand-ins (a fake Bot API, a simulated game server speaking the real wire format), and none of them connects to the game server. The pattern that dominates the later days is visible in the end-to-end runner tests: every live incident becomes a scenario that fails against the old code. Pass counts quoted in commits range from 118 world-model checks on 09-28 to 53,277/53,277 re-encoded server packets on 09-29 commit messages, git log afbbf71.

B.3Reverse-engineering and operations scripts

B.4Documents

CPacket, port and file-format reference

The protocol facts, packet ids, local ports and file formats the harness depends on, in one place. The chapters explain how each was found; this appendix is for looking things up.

All values are for the Outlands fork of ClassicUO (client 1.0.2.544, patched to 550 on 2026-09-28 without changing the wire), protocol version 12. Multi-byte packet fields are big-endian. The proprietary .uoo data files are little-endian. Sources are docs/PROTOCOL.md, docs/CIPHER.md, docs/MOVEMENT.md, docs/MAP.md and docs/MEMORY.md, by way of research briefs 02 and 03. For the stories behind them, see §3, §4 and §5.

C.1The wire in brief

C.2Ports and endpoints

C.3Client → server packets the harness sends

Every agent packet is built by harness/actions.py in the byte layout the stock client uses for the same gesture, padded to the client's length table. The counts are agent-originated packets across all 69 desktop session logs. For scale, the human's client sent 251,770 0xFF packets over the same logs, most of them keepalives.

Builders also exist for vendor sell (9F) and prompt and text-entry replies (9A, AC, C2). The login (91), character select (5D) and the keepalive are always the client's own.

C.4Server → client packets the harness reads

The world model has handlers for 46 S2C ids and 17 C2S ids. Every parsed id parses on every real packet in the 18 reference captures. The table groups the ones that matter by what the harness does with them.

The proxy also writes three kinds of packet to the client alone, encoded with the session key, which never reach the server. A 0x21 re-anchors the client's display after an agent step. A 0x6C cancel takes down a cursor the agent already answered. A 0xBF sub 4 closes a gump the agent already answered. Over the 69 desktop logs that came to 45,136, 5,688 and 1,875 packets respectively brief 02 §3.3. Why these exist is told in §3.

C.5File formats

DGlossary

Ultima Online, Outlands and project jargon used in this paper, alphabetically. Packet ids are in Appendix C.

Agent gate
The harness's pause button, kill switch, forced-break timer (about every 2 h, jittered) and 8 h/day budget. The proxy checks it before every injected packet; the human's own traffic is never gated.
Aspect
Outlands' gear-specialisation system. A full set of Harvest-aspect armor (hue 2086) adds effective skill and a chance of double yield, so the lumber runner checks it before every trip.
Bastet
A mounted player killer whose title line read "Serial Killer [Prevalia]". Bastet killed our lumberjacks three times on 10-02 and 10-03, which is where recall-on-sight came from (§8).
Board / log
Trees yield logs; logs are converted into boards, the stored product. On 2026-10-05 a regular board was worth about 26.8 gp.
Captcha
Outlands' anti-automation dialog for harvesters: a gump with a number to type, about every 5–10 minutes. Three wrong answers block harvesting for 6 h.
Characters
TestWorth (Test Shard, from 09-28), Hackworth (fresh Young character from 10-01), Shackleworth (an Arcane Mage, 10-03), Outland Dan (DTF guild, from 10-04), and Logan Wolf (holds the rental room; 0.37 h on 10-05, never agent-driven).
ClassicUO
The open-source UO client. Outlands ships its own fork of it, compiled with NativeAOT and with Razor built in.
Cliloc
The client's numbered table of localised strings (Cliloc.enu). Many server messages arrive as a cliloc number with arguments, e.g. 502406, "This book needs time to recharge."
ctl
harness/ctl.py, the command-line API through which the Seer (or a human) reads state, runs tasks, acts in game and answers junctures. Every call prints exactly one JSON object.
DTF
Outland Dan's guild. Its guild house holds a rune library of 36 tomes and 839 runes, and a house steward that leads to Logan Wolf's rental room, Dan's home.
Fastwalk key
A 32-bit token carried in each walk packet. The server hands tokens out (login usually ends on 8 and most re-arms carry 1, but the server also sends other small values; the proxy copies whatever it was given) and Outlands, unlike stock server emulators, checks them.
Gump
A server-defined dialog window: a layout of text, images, buttons and text entries. Runebooks, room menus, shelves and the captcha are all gumps.
Heat of Battle
The state after fighting a player, during which recall is blocked. It is one reason the harness never attacks players.
Juncture
An event on the overseer bus (table junctures) that can wake the Seer: a threat, a failed or finished task, nearby speech, a captcha, a death, possible staff. The store held 314 juncture rows by 2026-10-05.
Landing
The tile a recall arrives on. The planner picks the rune whose landing is nearest the chosen grove and remembers landings that went wrong.
Laya
An encoder model (ModernBERT-large, 421M parameters) that answers yes/no questions about a line of text in one forward pass. Here it triages speech heard near a harvest job ("is this an attendance check?"), served locally on the GPU and fine-tuned once.
Memory store
harness/data/harness.db, the SQLite file in which the harness keeps everything it experiences and learns: the event log, walk and harvest memory, trip rows, the overseer bus and the Seer's knowledge table. Runtime data, never committed (§5).
Moongate
A public teleporter with a destination menu. On Shelter Island, taking one asks the player to renounce Young status.
Multi
A many-piece structure, usually a house, that the server sends as one item whose graphic is an index into multi.mul. The harness expands multis into walls and doors so that routes stop running into houses.
NativeAOT
.NET's ahead-of-time compilation to native machine code. The Outlands client is not a managed assembly, so there is no plugin loading and no IL decompiler shortcut; reverse engineering went through Ghidra and the binary's reflection metadata.
Notoriety (noto)
A per-mobile reputation code in the mobile-update packet: 1 blue (innocent), 2 green (ally; the harness treats it as blue), 3–4 grey (attackable, criminal), 5 orange, 6 red (murderer), 7 invulnerable (NPCs, vendors, staff).
NPD
The New Player Dungeon on Shelter Island, where TestWorth's death demo took place and where the hunt runner first fought.
omp
The AI coding-agent harness that wrote this project. The Seer also runs on it, as an omp session or subagent.
Razor
The UO assistant (macros, hotkeys, scripts) built into the Outlands client and the only sanctioned automation. Razor scripts can't walk on Outlands (removed 2023-07), and Outlands can gate them from the server.
Recall
A Magery teleport to the location marked on a rune, cast as a spell or spent from a book's charges. It takes about 2 s and can be disturbed by damage. It is the harness's escape and its way to and from work.
Red / PK
A player killer. "Red" refers to notoriety 6, the murderer's name colour. Our threat model doesn't treat colour as proof either way: a thief looks blue until the moment of the steal.
Rental room
Outlands' inn-room housing. Nobody can follow you in and no recall reaches inside, so since 10-04 lumber trips end there.
Rune, runebook, rune tome
A rune marks one location to recall to. A runebook holds runes, recall charges and a default rune. A rune tome is a larger Outlands book (up to 26 rows) that opens only within 2 tiles.
Rune library
A collection of locked-down tomes others can use: the public Cambria library (14 tomes, 360 runes, including the 359 numbered Witcher runes) and the DTF guild house (36 tomes, 839 runes).
Secure chest
A locked-down container in the rental room that only its owners can open. Boards went there until the stockpile took over.
Seer, the
The LLM overseer: an omp agent session that supervises the deterministic runners through ctl, wakes on junctures, and talks to the owner in the viz and on Telegram. It was named on 2026-10-03 and given Hawkwind's voice (§9).
Shelter Island
Outlands' new-player island. Harvesting there needs Young status, halves the harvest chance and caps skills at 80, but no hostile player actions are possible.
Smart Harvest
Answering the hatchet's target cursor with yourself instead of a tree: the server then chops whatever harvestable tree is nearby. Adopted 2026-10-04.
Stationary Penalty
An Outlands rule: after a recall or teleport, or after about 5 minutes standing still, harvesting fails until you walk 5 steps.
Steward
The house NPC whose context menu ("Room" → "Visit Other Rooms") leads into a house's rental rooms. Leaving the room by its door returns you to the steward.
Stockpile
A Resource Stockpile: Outlands storage for raw materials, added to the room on 2026-10-05. It holds boards by kind and read 8,693 boards after the chest was emptied into it.
Storage shelf
A container that keeps a per-character loadout: "Resupply" tops the backpack up to it, "Restock" puts surplus and spent items back.
Test Shard
Outlands' public test server. Houses and inn rooms are wiped every day at midnight UTC. The project started there with TestWorth.
Trapped pouch
A pouch that explodes when opened. The runner stashes logs in one so that a thief who snoops it sets off an alarm: "a delay plus an alarm, not a lock".
Walk sequence
The 8-bit counter in every walk packet: starts at 0, wraps from 255 to 1, and the server accepts only the value it expects next. The proxy keeps one shared ladder for the human's and the agent's walks.
WinDivert
A Windows packet-diversion driver. The harness uses it as a small user-space NAT that redirects the client's port-2593 connection to the local proxy, because the client ignores its own server settings.
Witcher runes
A community rune set laid out by a player called Witcher for treasure hunting: about 359 numbered runes spread across the wilderness, publicly available in Cambria. They became the lumber planner's gateway to the whole map.
Young
New-player status. It protects starting items and gives access to Shelter's bank, vendors and harvesting. It is kept until you leave Shelter Island or renounce it, and renouncing is permanent.
